### Generated blocks [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/docs-builder.html#generated-blocks)

A page may hold a region the builder owns, marked in the Markdown source:

```text
<!-- generated:commands -->
...whatever the builder wrote last time...
<!-- /generated -->
```

`docs/docs.json` defines the blocks by name. Each block rewrites its region from the repo's own state: `json-table` and `symfony-commands` run a command from the repo root (a leading `php ` means the PHP binary, so the same file works on Windows, macOS and Linux) and render the command's JSON output, and `env` scans the source files for the environment variables the code reads.

#### The json-table type [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/docs-builder.html#the-json-table-type)

The `json-table` type runs its `run` command, takes the list at its `path` key from the JSON output, and renders a Markdown table: each column is `[heading, key]` or `[heading, key, "code"]` for a code span, a missing key gives an empty cell, booleans print `yes` or `no`, lists print comma separated, Symfony console style tags are stripped so a help cell reads plain, and pipes in a cell are escaped.

```json
{
    "blocks": {
        "hops": {
            "type": "json-table",
            "run": "php bin/booster hops --format=json",
            "path": "hops",
            "columns": [["Hop", "id", "code"], ["What it does", "summary"]]
        }
    }
}
```

#### The symfony-commands type [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/docs-builder.html#the-symfony-commands-type)

The `symfony-commands` type runs `<run> list --format=json` and renders the command reference: an overview table of command and description, then per command a heading at `level` (default 3), its description, one `Usage:` line per usage string, an Arguments table when it has arguments, and an Options table when it has options. An option prints its shortcut first (`-p`, `--path=VALUE`) and gets `=VALUE` only when it takes a value; its default prints in a code span, or stays empty when it is false. The built-in commands (`help`, `list`, `completion`, `_complete`) and hidden commands are skipped, and the application-level options (`--help`, `--quiet`, `--verbose`, `--version`, `--ansi`, `--no-ansi`, `--no-interaction`) are listed once, under "Options every command accepts".

```json
{
    "blocks": {
        "commands": {
            "type": "symfony-commands",
            "run": "php bin/console",
            "cli": "bin/console",
            "level": 3
        }
    }
}
```

#### The env type [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/docs-builder.html#the-env-type)

The `env` type walks the `scan` folders for quoted environment variable names that start with `prefix`, skips the names in `ignore` (an exact name, or a trailing `*` for a prefix), and renders one row per variable, sorted by name: its meaning and default from `describe` (a `[meaning, default]` pair) and the first file that reads it. A variable the code reads that `describe` does not list, and a variable `describe` lists that no scanned file reads, are findings.

```json
{
    "blocks": {
        "environment": {
            "type": "env",
            "scan": ["src", "config"],
            "prefix": "APP_",
            "ignore": ["APP_KEY"],
            "describe": {
                "APP_NAME": ["The app name", "Demo"],
                "APP_ENV": ["The environment", "production"]
            }
        }
    }
}
```

A plain run rewrites stale regions in the sources and then builds; `--check` reports a stale region instead of writing. A region whose name is not in `docs.json`, a block no page places, a block placed twice, and an opening marker with no closing marker are findings.

### Changelog page [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/docs-builder.html#changelog-page)

When `docs/nav.json` lists a page whose path is `changelog`, the builder owns `docs/changelog.md`: a plain run writes it from the repo's `CHANGELOG.md` before building, and `--check` never writes. The page takes the usual front matter (`title: "Changelog"` and a description), a marker comment naming its source, and the changelog's body with its top-level heading dropped, so every version heading stays as written: `## Unreleased`, `## [Unreleased]`, `## 0.5.0 (2026-11-03)` and `## [0.1.9] - 2026-11-03` all keep their shape and get the page's usual anchors. Links follow the site's rules: an `http(s)` link stays, a relative link becomes a blob link under the nav.json `source` when there is one, and loses its link, keeping its label, when there is not. The blob path follows the source's host: a GitHub source (`github.com` or `www.github.com`) gets `/blob/main/` (`https://github.com/acme/app/blob/main/README.md`) and any other host keeps GitLab's `/-/blob/main/` (`https://repo.example.com/acme/app/-/blob/main/README.md`). Links inside a code span or a fenced code block are left as written. A nav entry without a `CHANGELOG.md` is a finding, and a changed `CHANGELOG.md` or a missing `docs/changelog.md` is drift.

### Callouts [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/docs-builder.html#callouts)

A blockquote whose first line is a marker alone becomes a callout instead of a quotation:

```text
> [!NOTE]
> The body keeps the note.
```

The marker is case-insensitive and one of `[!NOTE]`, `[!TIP]`, `[!WARNING]` or `[!DANGER]`. The builder renders an `<aside>` with the classes `docs-callout` and `docs-callout--note` (one per kind), `role="note"`, a visible label, and the body below it, and drops the marker line from the body. A blockquote without a marker, or with a marker that is not one of the four, stays a plain blockquote. The kit's `docs.css` styles all four kinds from WayneUI tokens, in light and dark themes.

### Task lists [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/docs-builder.html#task-lists)

A GitHub task list item (`- [ ] Protect the default branch`) renders a disabled checkbox. The builder wraps the checkbox and the item's own text in a `<label class="docs-task">`, so the checkbox has an accessible name (axe's label rule) and is named by what it checks; a nested list or a second paragraph stays outside the label.

### What the check proves [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/docs-builder.html#what-the-check-proves)

- For a `symfony-commands` block, a code span or fenced line that starts with the CLI name must name a real command (`help` and `list` always pass), and every `--option` on it must be an option of that command or an application option; an unknown command or option is a finding.
- Every command and every option the CLI keeps must appear in the docs at least once (the generated block counts); a command or option nobody documented is a finding.
- A fenced block whose info string contains `docs-test: skip` is not scanned, and plain prose is never scanned.
- Every link a person wrote in the docs reaches something the site serves: a built page, a file under `site/`, or an external address; a relative link to a file the site does not serve (for example `../README.md`) is a finding.
- A fragment in a link must name a real heading on the page it points at, whether that is the page itself (`#setup`) or another built page (`guides/start.html#setup`); a missing id is a finding.
- Every image a page references (a Markdown image or an HTML `<img>`) must name a file under `docs/`, resolved against the source page's folder, and the build copies it byte for byte to the same relative path under `site/docs/` so the built page's relative src still resolves; a missing image is a finding, and unreferenced files are never copied.
- Every page carries the version stamp as a `docs-version` meta tag and in the footer, so a reader sees which release the docs describe.
- A `composer.json` with a `version` field must agree with the stamp; a different version is a finding.
- `--require-release` fails when `CHANGELOG.md` has no released heading yet, because the stamp would be `unreleased`.
- `--require-tag` fails when the repo's latest version tag does not match the stamp (a tag such as `v1.6.0` counts as `1.6.0`); the flag is off by default, so an untagged repo builds clean.
- When the nav lists a `changelog` page, `docs/changelog.md` mirrors `CHANGELOG.md` (front matter, marker comment, no top-level heading); a changed `CHANGELOG.md` or a missing page is drift, and a nav entry without a `CHANGELOG.md` is a finding.

### Tested examples [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/docs-builder.html#tested-examples)

`php bin/docs-site.php --examples` runs the tagged command examples in the docs and fails when reality drifts from what they promise. A fenced block whose info string is `bash run`, `sh run`, `console run` or `shell run` (optionally `exit=N`, default 0) is a command block: each non-empty line is a command (a leading `$ ` is stripped), run in order in a fresh temp copy of the `examples.cwd` folder; the next fenced block, when its info string is exactly `output`, is the expected output (stdout then stderr). Both sides are normalized before the comparison: CRLF to LF, trailing spaces trimmed per line, trailing blank lines removed, the example working directory and the repo root rewritten to the placeholders below, plus every regex rule in `examples.normalize`:

```text
<cwd>
<root>
```

Every shell block (bash, sh, shell, console, powershell or pwsh) must be tagged `run` or carry an HTML comment line reading `docs-test: skip REASON` directly before it; a block with neither, and a marker without a reason, are findings naming the file and line. Skips are counted and grouped by the words before the first comma, case-folded, in the one-line summary (`Examples: 7 run, 12 skipped (reasons: needs network 5, needs Docker 4)`), and `examples.maxSkips` in `docs/docs.json` caps them. The other keys of `examples` are optional: `cwd` names the repo folder copied into each example working directory, `alias` replaces a matching first word with another command (a leading `php ` means the PHP binary, a relative script path resolves against the repo root), `env` adds environment variables, and `timeout` caps each command in seconds (default 60). Generated-block regions are ignored, and a plain build and `--check` never run examples.

### JavaScript tests [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/docs-builder.html#javascript-tests)

The kit's `docs.js` carries its own tests in `tests/js/` (node:test with jsdom, pinned exactly in `package.json` and `package-lock.json`), and they run the same way locally and in CI. With Node 22 on the PATH:

```bash
npm ci && npm test
```

or, with only Docker:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/app" -w /app node:22-alpine sh -c "npm ci && npm test"
```

The `js-tests` job runs the same two commands on GitLab and GitHub. It stays out of `composer ci` because the PHP image has no Node.

---

Source: https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/doctor.html

## Doctor [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/doctor.html#doctor)

This page explains what `squire doctor` checks (the S-rules), how it hands off to PROCTOR, and how to read its output and exit codes. Next, read [Update and drift](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/update-and-drift.html) to fix the template drift doctor reports.

### What it checks [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/doctor.html#what-it-checks)

`squire doctor` checks an app against the best practices a machine can decide. It decides the rules below by reading the files in your repository. It never runs your app and never touches a server. A **fail** makes `doctor` exit 1; a **warn** or **info** does not. The numbers (S1 and so on) are the rule numbers from the WELD Citadel best-practices list; the list has more rules than a machine can decide, and those are not here.

Note

`squire doctor` checks deploy setup only; standards checks are PROCTOR's.

### The S-rules [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/doctor.html#the-s-rules)

| Rule | Level | What it checks | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S1 | fail | `build.sh` runs no `composer` or `npm` commands. | Citadel runs `build.sh` as root with only that file copied in; the source is not there. |
| S3 | warn | Every shell script has `set -e`; bash scripts also have `pipefail`. | A failing step must stop the script. |
| S4 | fail | No download is piped into a shell. | Pin a version and verify a checksum instead. |
| S8 | fail / warn | No CRLF in shell scripts (fail); `.gitattributes` forces LF for `*.sh` (warn). | CRLF breaks a script on Linux; Git on Windows adds it. |
| S9 | fail / warn | `scripts/release.sh` exists (fail); `build.sh` and a `deployments/` hook exist (warn); files match the template version (warn). | Build tooling, the one-time hook and the release script are three jobs. |
| S12 | fail | The release runs `composer install --no-dev`, never `composer update`, and uses `npm ci` or a frozen-lockfile install. | The lock file is the release contract. |
| S14 | warn | The release runs `proctor gate` or `proctor check`. | PROCTOR runs `composer audit` and the other app checks, so known-vulnerable dependencies show up in the deploy log. |
| S15 | fail / warn | `auth.json` is git-ignored (fail); Composer runs non-interactively (warn). | Credentials stay out of git; Citadel has no terminal to prompt on. |
| S16 | warn | Laravel: `php artisan optimize` runs in the release. | Config, route and view caches. |
| S17 | info | Laravel: `migrate --force` runs, or something else runs migrations. | Keep migrations compatible with the old code (parallel change). |
| S19 | warn | The release refuses to run as root; no `sudo` in scripts. | Files created as root cannot be written by the web process. |
| S20 | fail / warn | PROCTOR runs as a report (the command is followed by an OR branch that records the status), never as a bare command. | After a Quick Update the new commit is already live; a failing post-script cannot undo it. |
| S21 | warn | The release requests `/up` at the end. | A release that cannot answer a request did not ship. |
| S22 | warn | The release prints a marker per step. | The dashboard log shows where it stopped. |
| S35 | warn | The compose file uses a `citadel/php-apache` image. | Same PHP and extensions as production. |
| S36 | warn | A proxy that adds `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` is in front of the app. | Trusted-proxy and HTTPS detection bugs only show behind one. |
| S37 | warn | The local database is MySQL 5.6. | Its limits then show up locally. |
| S41 | fail | The Docker socket is not mounted. | It is root on the host. |
| S42 | warn | `.env` and `.env.squire` are git-ignored. | Secrets stay out of git. |
| S50 | info | Hand-off: points at `proctor check` for the lock file, composer audit and MySQL 5.6 checks, and names `proctor gate`, which the release asks for a go or no-go. | Each check has one owner; PROCTOR owns those, and `doctor` may run where PROCTOR is not installed. |
| S55 | fail / warn | A health check that does not run `artisan` or boot the framework exists. | Citadel runs it every 5 minutes as root. |
| S57 | warn | JavaScript packages install with `--ignore-scripts`; `.npmrc` sets `min-release-age`. | A compromised package cannot run at install time, and a version published an hour ago is not installed. |
| S67 | warn | Every image in the compose file is pinned by digest. | The same bytes tomorrow as today. |
| S70 | warn | Local containers drop capabilities and set `no-new-privileges`. | Least privilege, also locally. |
| S71 | warn | The local health check uses Citadel's timing (5 minutes, 15 seconds). | A slow `/up` shows up before it ships. |
| S78 | warn | A Vue app does not track `node_modules/` in git. | Dependencies are rebuilt from the lock file; the tree is not source. |

### Handoff to PROCTOR (S50) [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/doctor.html#handoff-to-proctor-s50)

The lock file (S13), composer audit and MySQL 5.6 safety (S18) are owned by PROCTOR; `doctor` no longer repeats them and hands off instead (S50). Each check has one owner; PROCTOR owns those, and `doctor` may run where PROCTOR is not installed.

Drift from the Squire templates is reported as a warning under S9, never as a failure: you may edit your copies.

`doctor` is a lint, not a gate. Wire it into CI if you want it to block; Squire does not decide that for you.

### Output [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/doctor.html#output)

`doctor` prints a text report by default, or a machine-readable one with `--format=json`.

```
vendor/bin/squire doctor [--path=.] [--format=text|json]
```

### Exit codes [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/doctor.html#exit-codes)

Exit codes: `0` pass, `1` findings (`init --check`: drift; `update`: an edited file still differs from the template; `doctor`: a failed rule), `2` the tool itself could not run.

---

Source: https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/image-hardening.html

## Image hardening [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/image-hardening.html#image-hardening)

This page lists what the kit's images harden, where each setting lives, and the switch that turns it down when an app needs that. Every item has a test that reads the file, and the [image contract suite](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/image-hardening.html#the-image-contract-suite) checks it again inside the built image. Read [Local parity](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/local-parity.html) first for the images themselves.

Two kinds of file carry the hardening. The **base** (`.squire/base-fallback.Dockerfile`) stands in for the Citadel image; what it sets is what Squire asks the real image to set, and the real image keeps deciding on Citadel. The **app image** (`.squire/Dockerfile`) is the local copy of the Dockerfile Citadel generates, and runs on either base.

### Apache: a quieter banner, no TRACE [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/image-hardening.html#apache-a-quieter-banner-no-trace)

The base enables `.squire/apache-hardening.conf` as `zz-squire-hardening.conf`, so it loads after Debian's `security.conf`, which ships `ServerTokens OS` and `ServerSignature On`:

| Directive | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `ServerTokens Prod` | The `Server` header says `Apache`, not `Apache/2.4.x (Debian)`. |
| `ServerSignature Off` | Error pages Apache writes itself carry no version footer. |
| `TraceEnable Off` | `TRACE` answers 405, so a script cannot read cookies back off an echo. |

These live in the base, never in the app image: locally the app image also runs on the real Citadel image, and hardening it there would show a parity the platform does not have.

### opcache: set by how your code arrives [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/image-hardening.html#opcache-set-by-how-your-code-arrives)

`.squire/php.ini` turns opcache on for the web (`opcache.enable = 1`, `opcache.enable_cli = 0`), and the fallback base loads the extension when its image does not already. Whether opcache looks at your files again depends on how the code gets into the container, so there are two cases and one switch, `SQUIRE_OPCACHE_VALIDATE`:

| How code arrives | `SQUIRE_OPCACHE_VALIDATE` | What opcache does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pulled into a running container: a Citadel Quick Update, a bind mount on your machine, or anywhere Squire cannot tell | `1`, the default | Checks a file again at most every 2 seconds (`revalidate_freq = 2`), so a release is served within 2 seconds with no restart. |
| Baked into an image that never changes: OpenShift, Coolify or raw Docker with the code copied in at build time | `0`, which you choose | Never checks a file again. The image is replaced, not edited, so there is nothing to notice, and requests skip the check. |

Set the switch where the image is built, `docker build --build-arg SQUIRE_OPCACHE_VALIDATE=0 -f .squire/Dockerfile .`, or when it runs, `-e SQUIRE_OPCACHE_VALIDATE=0` (the run-time value wins). Use `0` or `1`, never an empty value: PHP falls back to the default only when the variable is unset, and empty turns the checks off. Locally, put `SQUIRE_OPCACHE_VALIDATE=0` in `.env.squire` to try the baked case on your bind mount, and remember that saved files then wait for an Apache restart.

The other values, each read from the environment (PHP 8.3 and later):

| Setting | Default | Environment variable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `opcache.memory_consumption` | `128` (megabytes) | `SQUIRE_OPCACHE_MEMORY` |
| `opcache.max_accelerated_files` | `20000` (a Laravel app with its `vendor/` is 10000 to 15000 files) | `SQUIRE_OPCACHE_MAX_FILES` |
| `opcache.interned_strings_buffer` | `16` | none |

**The release warning stays.** The release script's "check opcache" step never fails, and says what it sees: a note when opcache checks files, and a warning when a release runs in place (Apache up) against an opcache set to `0`, because Apache keeps serving the PHP it compiled before the release until it restarts. In the first-release hook, before Apache starts, `0` is only a note.

Note

On Citadel the platform's own `php.ini` decides, not this file. Ask for the same as the kit's default: `validate_timestamps` on, `revalidate_freq` 2, because a Quick Update pulls code into the running container.

### disable_functions: the web loses the shell [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/image-hardening.html#disable-functions-the-web-loses-the-shell)

A web request should never shell out. `.squire/php-web.ini` holds the settings only the web server gets, and the app image appends it to `php.ini` as `php-apache2handler.ini`, the file mod_php reads instead of `php.ini`. The CLI reads `php.ini` alone, so Composer and its scripts, artisan, queue workers, the health check and the release script keep every function.

| Disabled on the web | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `exec`, `passthru`, `shell_exec`, `system` | Run a shell command: the first thing an injected payload reaches for. |
| `pcntl_exec` | Replaces the PHP process with another program. |
| `phpinfo`, `show_source`, `highlight_file` | Print the server's setup or its source to whoever asked. |

`proc_open` and `popen` stay: Symfony Mailer's sendmail transport, Laravel's `Process` and PHPMailer use them on the web. A test runs PHP on the same two files and checks both sides: the web list is gone, and the CLI and the mail functions are still there.

**The switch.** `SQUIRE_PHP_DISABLE_FUNCTIONS` replaces the list, and `none` (a name no function has) disables nothing: the way out for an older app that calls `exec` from a page while you move that work to a queued job. Leave it unset for the default list: PHP falls back only when the variable is unset, so an empty value disables nothing as well, and the parity compose files pass it by name only for that reason. Locally, put `SQUIRE_PHP_DISABLE_FUNCTIONS=none` in `.env.squire`.

`disable_classes` is not set. It never stopped a caller who could reach another class, and PHP 8.5 removed it.

Note

Like opcache, this is the kit's request: on Citadel the platform's own `php.ini` decides. A local run is stricter than Citadel until the platform adopts the list, which is the safe direction: an app that works locally works there.

### Session cookie: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/image-hardening.html#session-cookie-httponly-secure-samesite-lax)

PHP's own session cookie gets all three flags from `.squire/php.ini`, so a raw PHP app that never calls `helmet_boot()` still sends a safe one, and SESAME has nothing to warn about: `session.cookie_httponly = 1` (scripts cannot read it), `session.cookie_secure = 1` (https only; TLS ends at the proxy in front of the container, so the browser always sees https) and `session.cookie_samesite = Lax`.

Lax sends the cookie on a top-level GET from another site, which is how a CAS ticket and an OIDC code come back, and never on a cross-site POST, image or frame, which blunts CSRF. A SAML ACS receives a cross-site POST without the cookie; SESAME parks the response and finishes on a GET for that reason. An app whose session must ride some other cross-site POST sets `session.cookie_samesite` for that app instead. Laravel apps set their own cookie in `config/session.php` and are not affected. On Citadel, as above, the platform's `php.ini` decides.

### Secrets: files at run time, never in a layer [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/image-hardening.html#secrets-files-at-run-time-never-in-a-layer)

An image layer is readable by anyone who can pull the image, and `docker history` shows every build argument. So no secret is ever a build argument, an `ENV` line, a copied file, or something `build.sh` fetches. Tests hold the kit to it: the Dockerfiles carry no `ARG` or `ENV` named like a password, key, token or secret, the build context is `build.sh` and `.squire/` only (the `.dockerignore` starts with `*` and never lets an env file back in), and `build.sh` never reads `.env`.

Secrets arrive when the container runs:

| Where | How a secret arrives | Who reads it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Citadel | the dashboard's configuration-files step writes `./.env` into the source tree at deploy time | the app (Laravel, or phpdotenv in a raw PHP app); see [Citadel setup](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/citadel-setup.html) |
| Docker Compose | a `secrets:` entry, mounted as `/run/secrets/NAME` | the release script and the fallback entrypoint, below |
| `docker run` | `-v "$PWD/secrets/DB_PASSWORD:/run/secrets/DB_PASSWORD:ro"` | the same |
| OpenShift, Kubernetes | a Secret volume mounted at `/run/secrets` (each key is a file) | the same |

**The secrets folder.** `scripts/release.sh` and the fallback base's entrypoint share one loader: each regular file in `SQUIRE_SECRETS_DIR` (default `/run/secrets`) whose name is a variable name becomes that variable, with one trailing line ending trimmed, unless the environment already sets it. Names that would change how the shell runs (`PATH`, `IFS`, `BASH_ENV`, `LD_*` and a few more) are skipped, and a file the user cannot read is a warning. The log names what it loaded and never prints a value. The entrypoint loads the folder before Apache starts, so the PHP it runs sees the variables through `getenv()`; the release loads it again, because `su -l citadel` starts it with a clean environment.

Name the file after the variable the app reads. With Compose, set the file name with `target`:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    secrets:
      - source: db_password
        target: DB_PASSWORD
secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./secrets/db_password.txt
```

Note

The real Citadel image's entrypoint does not read `/run/secrets`; on Citadel, `./.env` is the secret path. Keep `./.env` and any `secrets/` folder out of git.

### npm: no install scripts, no day-old versions [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/image-hardening.html#npm-no-install-scripts-no-day-old-versions)

A package's install script runs with the release's rights, and a hijacked version is usually caught and pulled within hours. So the release does two things:

- **No install scripts.** `npm ci --ignore-scripts` (or `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts`), on by default with `SQUIRE_NPM_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=1`. A package that needs its own scripts (a native addon such as `sharp`, a binary download such as `esbuild`) is named in `SQUIRE_NPM_REBUILD`, and only it runs them after the install: `npm rebuild --ignore-scripts=false sharp`, or `pnpm rebuild sharp` (pnpm 10 also needs it in `pnpm.onlyBuiltDependencies`). Each name is checked against the shape of a package name first.
- **A minimum release age.** The Vue layer's `.npmrc` sets `min-release-age=1`: `npm install` and `npm update` skip versions published less than a day ago, so they never reach the lock file. `npm ci` installs the lock exactly, so this guards the day the lock is written, not the release. npm reads the setting from 11.10 on; Node 22 ships npm 10, which ignores it, and the release says so in its log.

**Policy.** Keep one day for every app; raise it, never lower it, in the app's own `.npmrc`. To take a fix published this morning, install it on purpose and review the lock diff:

```sh
npm install --min-release-age=0 some-package@1.2.3
```

### Base images: pinned by digest [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/image-hardening.html#base-images-pinned-by-digest)

A tag such as `php:8.4-apache` moves: two builds of the same commit a week apart can get different bytes. Every image the kit's files pull is pinned by the digest of its multi-arch list instead, `php:8.4.27-apache@sha256:...`, which names the same bytes on an arm64 laptop or CI runner and on an amd64 server: the fallback base's PHP, Node and Composer, the Vue layer's Node service, HA-Proxy and MySQL in the compose files, and the Oracle parity bases. A test fails on any reference without a digest.

The kit's Composer (the fallback base and the Oracle parity image) is 2.11.1, `composer:2.11.1@sha256:8de2184c...`; 2.10 is no longer maintained. Composer 2.11's `policy.cooldown` is off by default, and the kit does not turn it on.

The kit's Dockerfiles write each name in full, registry and namespace included: `docker.io/library/php:8.4.27-apache@sha256:...`, not `php:8.4.27-apache@sha256:...`. Docker reads both the same way, but Buildah and Podman refuse a short name where their short-name mode is enforcing (a `COPY --from=composer:2` fails outright), so a CI job that builds with Buildah needs the full name. A test fails on a short name in any of the kit's Dockerfiles.

#### Through a proxy or a mirror [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/image-hardening.html#through-a-proxy-or-a-mirror)

The fallback base takes its three images as build arguments, `PHP_IMAGE`, `NODE_IMAGE` and `COMPOSER_IMAGE`, and Composer comes from a `FROM ${COMPOSER_IMAGE} AS composer` stage, so nothing has to be edited in the file. To pull through a proxy or a mirror, keep each default's tag and digest and swap the registry part. GitLab's Dependency Proxy takes the Docker Hub name without `docker.io/library/` after its group prefix:

```sh
base=.squire/base-fallback.Dockerfile
prefix="$CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_GROUP_IMAGE_PREFIX"
args=""
for arg in PHP_IMAGE NODE_IMAGE COMPOSER_IMAGE; do
  ref=$(sed -n "s/^ARG $arg=//p" "$base")
  args="$args --build-arg $arg=$prefix/${ref#docker.io/library/}"
done
docker build -f "$base" $args -t squire/php-parity-base:8.4 .squire   # or: buildah bud ...
```

A registry mirror that keeps Docker Hub's paths takes the same loop with `$mirror/library/${ref#docker.io/library/}`. The digest still decides the bytes, so a proxy cannot hand back a different image under the same name.

To bump one, read the new list's digest and check it lists both platforms, then replace the whole reference:

```sh
docker buildx imagetools inspect php:8.4.28-apache
```

Look for the `Digest:` line, and for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64/v8` under Manifests. Then run the tests and the image contract suite on both platforms. Maintainers have the full procedure in `MAINTAINING.md`. Two references are yours, not the kit's: the real Citadel image (`SQUIRE_BASE_IMAGE`, pin it once you have its digest) and any `SQUIRE_NODE_IMAGE`, `SQUIRE_PROXY_IMAGE` or `SQUIRE_MYSQL_IMAGE` override.

### The image contract suite [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/image-hardening.html#the-image-contract-suite)

A file can promise anything; the running image is what counts. `scripts/contract-image.sh` (in Squire's repository) builds the fallback base and the app image for a platform, runs the container with a throwaway raw PHP app mounted at `/citadel/src` and a throwaway secret mounted at `/run/secrets`, runs the release as `citadel`, and then pipes `scripts/contract-image-checks.php` to `php` inside the container. One PASS or FAIL line per check:

| Item | Checked in the running image |
| --- | --- |
| Apache | the `Server` header is exactly `Apache`; no `X-Powered-By`; `TRACE` answers 405 with no version footer |
| opcache | code pulled in place: the web checks files (`validate_timestamps` 1, `revalidate_freq` 2) and the release notes it; code baked in (the app image rebuilt with `SQUIRE_OPCACHE_VALIDATE=0`): the web never checks; 20000 files either way |
| disable_functions | the web has no `exec` and the rest, and keeps `proc_open` and `popen`; the CLI disables nothing; a Composer `post-install-cmd` that shells out runs in the release |
| Secrets | the web sees the mounted secret (compared as an md5, never printed), the release names it, and its value is in no log, no layer and no image config |

```sh
sh scripts/contract-image.sh --platform=linux/amd64
sh scripts/contract-image.sh --platform=linux/arm64   # needs qemu emulation on an amd64 host
```

GitHub CI runs it for both platforms on every push. It proves the fallback base, not the real Citadel image, which is internal: a green run is a contract, not a certificate.

---

Source: https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/local-parity.html

## Local parity [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/local-parity.html#local-parity)

This page sets up the local kit: your app on the Citadel image, behind an HA-Proxy that adds the same forwarding headers, with MySQL 5.6.51 beside it. Finish [Citadel setup](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/citadel-setup.html) first if you have not run `squire init` yet.

### Requirements [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/local-parity.html#requirements)

Needs Docker with Compose v2. Windows needs Docker Desktop with the WSL 2 backend; no shell other than PowerShell is required.

**On Windows, keep the source in the WSL 2 filesystem.** Advice, not a requirement: keep the app's source tree inside the WSL 2 Linux filesystem (for example under `~/src` in your WSL distribution) and run `scripts/parity.sh` from there, not from a Windows folder such as `C:\Users\you\...` reached through `/mnt/c`. Bind mounts from the Windows side are much slower (Composer and npm installs feel it most), and file ownership and permissions do not map cleanly; that is the cause of the `Permission denied` failure described under the bind-mount question (OPEN_QUESTIONS 15). The PowerShell `scripts\parity.ps1` still works from a Windows folder, only slower.

### Engines and licenses [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/local-parity.html#engines-and-licenses)

Squire needs any engine that runs Docker Compose v2 compatible files. The ones named here:

- **Docker Engine on Linux**: open source, Apache 2.0.
- **Docker Desktop on Windows** with the WSL 2 backend: a commercial product, free for small business, personal and educational use, and paid for larger organizations, so check your own license.
- **Podman** with a Compose v2 compatible provider, and **Colima** on macOS: expected to work, not tested here.

Only Docker Desktop and Docker Engine have been run.

### Starting parity [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/local-parity.html#starting-parity)

```sh
# Linux and macOS
cp .env.squire.example .env.squire     # then set the passwords
scripts/parity.sh up                   # or: scripts/parity.sh up --fallback

# Windows (PowerShell 5.1 or 7)
Copy-Item .env.squire.example .env.squire
scripts\parity.ps1 up                  # or: scripts\parity.ps1 up -Fallback
```

Commands: `up`, `down`, `reset` (also removes volumes), `logs [service]`, `shell [service]`, `status`, `pin` (prints the digests of the images you have pulled, so you can pin them).

### What it starts [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/local-parity.html#what-it-starts)

It starts the app container from the Citadel image (built by Citadel's `build_images` command, or pulled from wherever you keep it) with your source mounted at `/citadel/src`, runs your `deployments/` as the `citadel` user the way Citadel does, and puts an HA-Proxy in front that adds the same forwarding headers. MySQL 5.6.51 is reachable from the app as host `mysql` and from your machine on `127.0.0.1:3307`. Containers drop capabilities, set `no-new-privileges`, and carry memory and process limits. The database port is bound to loopback only. The Vue layer's compose file adds a Node 22 service, pinned to the same major as the Citadel image, for frontend tooling.

The compose file's `portable` profile starts nothing on a plain `up`. Named, it runs [the portable image](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/portable-image.html) instead: the code baked in, one image as `migrate`, `web`, `worker` and `scheduler`, as a non-root user in group 0 on 8080, the way a platform other than Citadel runs it.

### No access to the real image? [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/local-parity.html#no-access-to-the-real-image)

`--fallback` builds an approximation from the official `php` image plus Citadel's extensions. It is good for trying Squire out and not for proving parity. If the build step fails with a permission error writing `vendor/`, the source folder is not writable by the container's `citadel` user (uid 1000 by default); on Linux set `SQUIRE_SOURCE_UID` and `SQUIRE_SOURCE_GID` to yours.

Note

The compose file refuses to start without the two passwords. Set them in `.env.squire` after copying `.env.squire.example`; the example holds placeholders only.

### Next [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/local-parity.html#next)

Read [The release script](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/release-script.html) for what runs inside the app container, or [Citadel setup](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/citadel-setup.html) for the dashboard side of the same pipeline.

---

Source: https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html

## MySQL upgrade path [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#mysql-upgrade-path)

The shared database is MySQL 5.6.51, the last 5.6 release (2021-01-05). Oracle moved 5.6 to Sustaining Support on 2021-02-01, so the server has had no fixes for nearly six years, and Laravel 13 does not support it (its floor is MySQL 5.7). This page is the path off it: three hops, 5.6 to 5.7 to 8.0 to 8.4 LTS, and for each one the check to run first, the backup to take, what your app's driver and framework need, and how to get back if the hop goes wrong.

It is written for a developer who has never upgraded MySQL. You will not run the server upgrade yourself; you will get your app and its data ready for it, rehearse it on a copy, and know your way back. A squire does not ride into the joust, but the knight goes nowhere without a squire who checked the straps.

### The path, and why it has three hops [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#the-path-and-why-it-has-three-hops)

MySQL supports upgrading one release series at a time. Its manual says an upgrade that skips a series is not supported, and names 5.6 straight to 8.0 as the example; 5.7 straight to 8.4 is not a supported step either ([8.0 upgrade paths](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/upgrade-paths.html), [8.4 upgrade paths](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/upgrade-paths.html)). So:

| Hop | From | To | Why this stop |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 5.6.51 | 5.7 | The next series. Laravel 13's floor. |
| 2 | 5.7 | 8.0 | The next series. 8.0 left extended support on 2026-04-30, so it is a stepping stone, never a place to stay. |
| 3 | 8.0 | 8.4 LTS | The target. Premier support to 2029, extended support to 2032 ([endoflife.date](https://endoflife.date/mysql)). |

The path stops at 8.4. MySQL 9.7 became the next LTS on 2026-04-21, and the 8.4 manual lists "next LTS series" as a supported step, so 8.4 to 9.7 would be a fourth hop later. Whether the plan continues to 9.7 is an open decision, and this guide does not make it. Whether PHP's MySQL drivers and Laravel are tested against 9.7 has not been checked.

Whether one app can skip the hops by dumping its own database from 5.6 and loading it into a fresh 8.4 server has not been confirmed. That is an experiment, recorded [at the end of this page](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#the-dump-to-fresh-server-experiment); until it has a result, plan on the three hops.

### Before you start [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#before-you-start)

- [ ] You know which schemas on the server are your app's, and who else shares the server.
- [ ] You can make a copy: a scratch server you are allowed to break, where your dump can be restored. A Docker container on your machine is fine.
- [ ] Your app's test suite runs against a real MySQL, not only SQLite. SQLite passes code that MySQL rejects.
- [ ] You have read the hop you are preparing for, below, and the rollback for it.
- [ ] You have taken a backup **and restored it once** on the copy. A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup.
- [ ] You have run [the pre-upgrade script](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#the-pre-upgrade-script) on that copy and worked through what it lists.

### Three tools you will use [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#three-tools-you-will-use)

**MySQL Shell's upgrade checker**, `util.checkForServerUpgrade()`, is the authority on what blocks an upgrade. Use the MySQL Shell of the version you are moving *to*: tried on empty test servers for this guide, Shell 8.4 refused to check a server at its own version or higher, and refused a 5.6 server outright ("this tool requires server to be at least at version 5.7"). So it helps from hop 2 on. The official `mysql:8.4` Docker image ships `mysqlsh`.

**`mysqlcheck --all-databases --check-upgrade`** is the table check the 8.0 prerequisites page names beside the Shell checker, and the one of the two that runs on a 5.6 source. The `mysql:5.6.51` image ships it; the `mysql:8.4` image does not.

**Squire's pre-upgrade script**, `scripts/mysql-preupgrade-checks.sql`, lists four things in your schema that the hops are known to trip on. It is a quick first look, not a replacement for the checker.

### The pre-upgrade script [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#the-pre-upgrade-script)

[`scripts/mysql-preupgrade-checks.sql`](https://github.com/waynestate/squire/blob/main/scripts/mysql-preupgrade-checks.sql) is read-only: every statement is a `SELECT` over `information_schema`, or a `SET SESSION` that changes only its own connection. A test in Squire's suite fails if anything else creeps in. Run it on your copy anyway, never on the shared server: on a busy server those scans are slow, and the copy is where you fix what it finds.

Every check returns the same four columns, `check_name`, `schema_name`, `object_name` and `detail`. A check that finds nothing prints nothing.

| Check | What it lists | Matters for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `old_temporal_columns` | `TIME`, `DATETIME` and `TIMESTAMP` columns still in the pre-5.6.4 storage format. They stop an in-place upgrade to 8.0; `REPAIR TABLE` rebuilds them. | Hops 1 and 2 |
| `long_names_over_64` | Foreign key names and view column names that show 64 characters or more. 8.0 refuses names over 64. `information_schema` may cut a longer name to 64, so anything at 64 is listed too: confirm it with `SHOW CREATE TABLE` or `SHOW CREATE VIEW`. | Hop 2 |
| `charset_not_utf8mb4` | Tables whose collation is not `utf8mb4_unicode_ci`, Laravel's default. Not a blocker by itself, a decision to make on purpose (see hop 2). | Hop 2 |
| `rejected_by_8_4` | Foreign keys whose referenced columns are not exactly one whole `PRIMARY` or `UNIQUE` key (a plain index, part of a composite key, a prefix index), and `AUTO_INCREMENT` on `FLOAT` or `DOUBLE`. | Hop 3 |

Run it from the root of a Squire checkout with any MySQL client. `--force` matters: on 8.0 and later the last check's `SET` fails with "Unknown system variable 'show_old_temporals'" (that variable exists on 5.6 and 5.7 only), and `--force` lets the client carry on. Nothing is lost: an 8.0 server has no old temporal columns to find.

```sh
# Any mysql client, from the root of a Squire checkout
mysql --force --table -h "$COPY_HOST" -P "$COPY_PORT" -u "$COPY_USER" -p < scripts/mysql-preupgrade-checks.sql

# No client installed: use the one in the mysql:8.4 image (Linux, macOS, or PowerShell)
docker run --rm -it -v "${PWD}/scripts:/checks:ro" mysql:8.4 \
  sh -c 'mysql --force --table -h "$0" -P "$1" -u "$2" -p < /checks/mysql-preupgrade-checks.sql' \
  "$COPY_HOST" "$COPY_PORT" "$COPY_USER"
```

In PowerShell, put the `docker run` on one line (or end each line with a backtick instead of `\`), and set `$COPY_HOST` and the others as PowerShell variables first. PowerShell has no `<` redirection, which is why the redirection runs inside the container.

For this guide the script ran clean against an empty 5.6.51 server and an empty 8.4.13 server, and the 8.4 client ran it against the 5.6 server. On a seeded test schema it listed a `latin1` table, a foreign key on a non-unique index, a foreign key on part of a composite primary key, an `AUTO_INCREMENT DOUBLE` column, and a 64-character foreign key name and view column, and it skipped the foreign keys that reference a whole key. The `old_temporal_columns` check could not be seeded, because 5.6.4 and later only create the new format; the `5.5 binary format` marker it looks for is not verified on a real old table.

### What a backup means here [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#what-a-backup-means-here)

For each hop, the backup is a **logical dump made with the source server's own client version**: dump a 5.6.51 server with the 5.6.51 `mysqldump`, a 5.7 server with the 5.7 one, and so on. A dump is plain SQL you can read, load into a fresh server, and keep beside the release that was live when you took it. The Docker image of the source version is the easy way to get the matching client:

```sh
# Before hop 1: a 5.6.51 dump of your app's schema, written to the current folder
docker run --rm -it -v "${PWD}:/backup" mysql:5.6.51 \
  mysqldump --host="$SOURCE_HOST" --user="$SOURCE_USER" --password \
    --single-transaction --routines --triggers --events \
    --databases your_app --result-file=/backup/your_app-5.6.51.sql
```

That command ran against a 5.6.51 test server for this guide. `--single-transaction` gives a consistent snapshot of InnoDB tables without locking them, and `--routines`, `--triggers` and `--events` bring the stored code along; those descriptions come from mysqldump's own help, and whether your schema needs more (users and grants, for one, live in the `mysql` schema, which this dump leaves out) is not verified here. Name each file after the version that made it, so a rollback never loads the wrong one.

Then restore it once, on a fresh server of the **same** version, and run your app's tests against it. That is the rehearsal that makes it a backup.

### Rollback, for every hop [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#rollback-for-every-hop)

MySQL cannot go back in place. The 8.4 manual's downgrading page allows an in-place downgrade only within one LTS series (8.4.y to an earlier 8.4.x). Going back from 8.4 to 8.0 works only by logical dump and load or by replication, and is "only supported for rollback purposes" when no new server features have been applied to the data. Downgrading to 5.7 or earlier is not supported at all. So there is no "install the old version over the new one": every rollback below is one of two shapes.

1. **Restore the pre-hop dump to a fresh server of the old version.** Simple and always available. Anything written after the hop is not in that dump, so it is lost unless you export it separately; keep the window between the hop and the decision short.
2. **Keep a server one hop behind.** Leave the old-version server (or a replica of it) running, untouched, beside the new one, so going back is a switch of the app's `DB_HOST` and not a restore. It stops receiving writes at the hop. Replication from the new server back to the old one, which would carry those writes, is documented only for the 8.4 to 8.0 rollback; for the earlier hops it is not verified.

Decide which shape each hop uses before the window, write down who flips the switch, and rehearse it on the copy. A rollback nobody has tried is the same as no rollback.

### Hop 1: 5.6.51 to 5.7 [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#hop-1-5-6-51-to-5-7)

The smallest hop for your code and the biggest for your safety: everything after it is a supported Laravel 13 database.

#### Check first [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#check-first)

- Run `mysqlcheck --all-databases --check-upgrade` with the 5.6.51 client against your copy. MySQL Shell's checker refuses a 5.6 source (see [the tools](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#three-tools-you-will-use)).
- Run [the pre-upgrade script](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#the-pre-upgrade-script). Rebuild any `old_temporal_columns` now; they block hop 2, and the copy is the place to time how long `REPAIR TABLE` takes on your biggest tables.
- Whether `mysql_upgrade` must run after an in-place 5.6 to 5.7 upgrade is not covered by this guide's sources and is not verified.

#### Back up [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#back-up)

A `mysqldump` from the 5.6.51 client, [as above](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#what-a-backup-means-here), restored once on a fresh 5.6.51 server. Squire's [local parity](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/local-parity.html) kit already runs MySQL 5.6.51, so it can be that fresh server.

#### Driver and Laravel floor [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#driver-and-laravel-floor)

- **Laravel 13** lists MySQL 5.7 and later, and needs PHP 8.3 or later. After this hop your app is on a supported database for the first time.
- **PHP** connects to 5.6 with `mysql_native_password` (the accounts on a stock 5.6.51 server use it), which mysqlnd supports. What 5.7 accounts default to is not covered by this guide's sources.
- **TLS**: 5.6 servers older than 5.6.46 speak only TLS 1.0; 5.6.46 and later add TLS 1.1 and 1.2 on OpenSSL builds. Those facts come from search snippets of the 5.6 manual, so they are partly verified. If your PHP host enforces a TLS 1.2 floor, test the connection on each hop. Laravel only sets TLS options when `MYSQL_ATTR_SSL_CA` is set.
- **What you may start using after the hop** (and not before): JSON columns (5.7.8), generated columns (5.7.6), `renameIndex` (5.7). Keep `Schema::defaultStringLength(191)` in `AppServiceProvider::boot()` for now: a 5.6 server's defaults are `innodb_large_prefix` off and the Antelope file format (both flipped in 5.7.7) and DYNAMIC rows became the default only in 5.7.9, so tables created on 5.6 still have the 767-byte index limit. Whether an in-place upgrade changes their row format is not verified.

#### Rollback [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#rollback)

Restore the 5.6.51 dump to a fresh 5.6.51 server, or keep the 5.6.51 server running beside the 5.7 one ([the two shapes](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#rollback-for-every-hop)). A 5.7 server cannot be turned back into 5.6 in place.

### Hop 2: 5.7 to 8.0 [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#hop-2-5-7-to-8-0)

The hop with the most changes, and 8.0 is out of support, so plan hop 3 before you start this one.

#### Check first [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#check-first-1)

- Run MySQL Shell's `util.checkForServerUpgrade()` from Shell 8.0 or 8.4 against your 5.7 copy, and `mysqlcheck --all-databases --check-upgrade`. Then work through the [8.0 upgrade prerequisites](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/upgrade-prerequisites.html).
- Run [the pre-upgrade script](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#the-pre-upgrade-script). For this hop, `old_temporal_columns` and `long_names_over_64` are blockers; `charset_not_utf8mb4` is a decision.
- Other blockers the prerequisites page names: `ENUM` or `SET` elements over 255 characters, new reserved words, table names that clash with 8.0's data dictionary, partitioned tables on engines other than InnoDB, and obsolete SQL modes, which stop the server from starting. "Only upgrade a MySQL server instance that was properly shut down": a server that crashed needs a clean shutdown (`innodb_fast_shutdown=0`) first. Names over 64 characters could not even be created on 5.6.51 or 8.4 when tried for this guide, so on a 5.6 source `long_names_over_64` should find nothing new; it matters for objects created on 5.7.

#### Character set and collation, on purpose [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#character-set-and-collation-on-purpose)

From 8.0 the server's default character set is `utf8mb4` and its default collation `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci`. The new collations are NO PAD where the old ones are PAD SPACE, so trailing spaces start to matter in `VARCHAR` comparisons. A changed default does not alter existing columns, but converting a column can make two rows equal that were not (MySQL's own example is Örebro and Orebro) and fail with a duplicate-key error, can rebuild indexes under a table lock, and can hit the 3072-byte key limit ([migrating from older collations](https://dev.mysql.com/blog-archive/mysql-8-0-collations-migrating-from-older-collations/)).

So before this hop: record every table's character set and collation (the script's `charset_not_utf8mb4` lists the ones that are not Laravel's default; a stock 5.6.51 server defaults to `latin1`, so tables made without a charset are `latin1`), set `charset` and `collation` explicitly on the app's connection in `config/database.php` and in its migrations, and run MySQL's duplicate-key check before converting anything. Never use the 8.0-only `utf8mb4_0900_*` collations while any server in the path is older than 8.0.

#### Back up [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#back-up-1)

A `mysqldump` from the 5.7 client, restored once on a fresh 5.7 server.

#### Driver and Laravel floor [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#driver-and-laravel-floor-1)

- **Authentication**: `caching_sha2_password` is the 8.0 server default. PHP supports it fully from 7.4.4, so PHP 8.3 to 8.5 connects. Connect each app to an 8.0 test server before the move anyway.
- **Laravel 13** keeps working, and some of its paths get better: the database queue uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` on 8.0.1 and later, so parallel workers stop contending. Window functions and CTEs in raw SQL, descending indexes and enforced `CHECK` constraints (8.0.16) arrive here. Do not use any of them until every server your app can land on is 8.0 or later.
- **Tests**: run your suite against 5.7 and 8.0 during the transition. The shared server moves every app at once, so apps must be ready before the move, not after.

#### Rollback [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#rollback-1)

Restore the 5.7 dump to a fresh 5.7 server, or keep the 5.7 server running beside the 8.0 one. MySQL does not support downgrading to 5.7 or earlier, and loading an 8.0 dump into 5.7 is not verified.

### Hop 3: 8.0 to 8.4 LTS [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#hop-3-8-0-to-8-4-lts)

The last hop, onto a series with years of fixes ahead of it.

#### Check first [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#check-first-2)

- Run MySQL Shell 8.4's `util.checkForServerUpgrade()` against your 8.0 copy (the `mysql:8.4` image has it).
- Run [the pre-upgrade script](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#the-pre-upgrade-script) and fix everything `rejected_by_8_4` lists. 8.4 rejects foreign keys on non-unique or partial keys unless `restrict_fk_on_non_standard_key` is `OFF` (it is `ON` on a stock 8.4.13 server), and an `AUTO_INCREMENT` column on `FLOAT` or `DOUBLE` makes the upgrade fail (a stock 8.4.13 server also refuses to create one).
- Search your app for the rest of what 8.4 changes ([what is new in 8.4](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/mysql-nutshell.html)):
  - accounts that use `mysql_native_password`, which 8.4 turns off by default (a stock 8.4.13 server shows the plugin `DISABLED`). On the 8.0 copy, `SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user WHERE plugin = 'mysql_native_password'` lists them;
  - `default_authentication_plugin` in any server config: the option is removed, and a config that sets it fails to start;
  - `MANUAL`, `PARALLEL` and `QUALIFY` used as unquoted names;
  - old replication statements such as `START SLAVE`, which are removed.
- Several InnoDB defaults change, including `innodb_adaptive_hash_index` to `OFF` and `innodb_flush_method` to `O_DIRECT` (both confirmed on a stock 8.4.13 server). They affect performance: time your heaviest pages and jobs on the copy.

#### Back up [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#back-up-2)

A `mysqldump` from the 8.0 client, restored once on a fresh 8.0 server.

#### Driver and Laravel floor [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#driver-and-laravel-floor-2)

- **Authentication**: connect each app to an 8.4 test server before the move. A client that can only use `mysql_native_password` fails to connect. PHP 8.3 to 8.5 supports `caching_sha2_password`, so the PHP side is ready; the account on the server must use it too.
- **Laravel 13**: no floor change; it supports 5.7 and later. PHP 8.5 deprecates the `PDO::MYSQL_ATTR_*` constants for `Pdo\Mysql::ATTR_*`, and Laravel 13's config already handles both.

#### Rollback [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#rollback-2)

This is the one hop with a documented way back other than a restore. Going from 8.4 to 8.0 works by logical dump and load or by replication, "only supported for rollback purposes" and only while no new 8.4 server features have been applied to the data. So: restore the 8.0 dump to a fresh 8.0 server, or keep an 8.0 server one hop behind, fed by replication from 8.4, until you are sure. Do not adopt 8.4-only features until the rollback window has closed.

### After 8.4 [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#after-8-4)

Stay on 8.4 and take its patch releases (the latest was 8.4.13, 2026-09-30); an in-place move within the 8.4 series, up or down, is supported. Whether to continue to 9.7 LTS is an open decision (see [the path](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#the-path-and-why-it-has-three-hops)).

### The dump-to-fresh-server experiment [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#the-dump-to-fresh-server-experiment)

The open question: can one app dump its own schema from 5.6.51 (with the 5.6.51 client) and load it straight into a fresh 8.4 server, skipping the hops for that app's data? MySQL documents the series-by-series path for upgrading a server, and this shortcut is not confirmed. The experiment loads a real app's dump into a fresh 8.4 server, runs its migrations and test suite against it, and records what failed. Until it has a result here, follow the three hops.

#### Result [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#result)

### Not verified [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#not-verified)

These statements on this page are not backed by the sources below or by a run for this guide:

- Whether `mysql_upgrade` must run after the 5.6 to 5.7 in-place upgrade.
- Whether an in-place 5.6 to 5.7 upgrade changes the row format of existing tables.
- Replication from a newer server back to an older one for hops 1 and 2.
- Whether the mysqldump options shown are all a schema needs (users and grants are left out).
- The `5.5 binary format` marker on a real pre-5.6.4 table.
- The 5.6 TLS versions (from search snippets of the manual only).
- PHP driver and Laravel support for MySQL 9.7.
- The dump-to-fresh-server shortcut.

### Sources [#](https://squire.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/mysql-upgrade-path.html#sources)

- MySQL: [8.0 upgrade paths](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/upgrade-paths.html), [8.4 upgrade paths](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/upgrade-paths.html), [8.4 upgrading](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/upgrading.html), [8.0 upgrade prerequisites](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/upgrade-prerequisites.html), [what is new in 8.4](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/mysql-nutshell.html), [what is new in 8.0](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/mysql-nutshell.html), [migrating from older collations](https://dev.mysql.com/blog-archive/mysql-8-0-collations-migrating-from-older-collations/), [5.7.7 release notes](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/relnotes/mysql/5.7/en/news-5-7-7.html), [5.7.9 release notes](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/relnotes/mysql/5.7/en/news-5-7-9.html), [EOL notices](https://www.mysql.com/support/eol-notice.html).
- Support dates: [endoflife.date MySQL](https://endoflife.date/mysql).
- Laravel 13: [database](https://laravel.com/docs/13.x/database), [release notes](https://laravel.com/docs/13.x/releases).
- PHP: [MySQL 8 and `caching_sha2_password`](https://www.php.net/manual/en/mysqli.requirements.php), [PDO MySQL](https://www.php.net/manual/en/ref.pdo-mysql.php).
- Runs for this guide: throwaway `mysql:5.6.51` and `mysql:8.4` (8.4.13, MySQL Shell 8.4.10) containers, empty and with a small seeded schema, on 2026-11-09. No real server was touched.
